stem: Which environmental-cleaning practice is appropriate between procedures in an operating room?

options.A: Clean only when visible soil is present or a known infection has been identified
options.B: Skip environmental cleaning if sterile technique will be used for the next case
options.C: Clean and disinfect designated environmental surfaces and noncritical equipment according to the between-procedure protocol
options.D: Perform only terminal cleaning after the final procedure of the day

rationale: CDC environmental-cleaning guidance identifies operating rooms as areas requiring environmental cleaning at three intervals: before the first procedure, between procedures, and after the last procedure. The OR section applies to environmental surfaces and surfaces of noncritical equipment; critical and semicritical equipment require separate specialized reprocessing. C is correct.
educational_objective: Recognize routine between-procedure environmental cleaning as a required infection-prevention practice in operating rooms.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_version_date: Current CDC healthcare environmental-cleaning webpage accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: Section 4.6.1 Operating rooms — environmental cleaning before first procedure, between procedures, and after last procedure; environmental surfaces/noncritical equipment
source_claim_supported: Operating rooms require environmental cleaning between procedures; the described process covers environmental surfaces and noncritical equipment surfaces, while critical/semicritical equipment requires specialized reprocessing.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — environmental infection-control practices
blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — environmental cleaning

source_original.stem: Between surgical cases, why is cleaning and disinfection of operating-room environmental surfaces performed?

options.A: Only to improve room appearance after procedures involving visibly contaminated equipment
options.B: To replace sterile technique during the next procedure once environmental cleaning is complete
options.C: To reduce environmental bioburden and the opportunity for pathogen transmission between cases
options.D: Only after a client with a known infection leaves the room, rather than after routine procedures

source_original.rationale: Between-case environmental cleaning and disinfection reduces contamination of high-touch and procedure-area surfaces and is one component of infection prevention. It complements rather than replaces aseptic and sterile technique.
source_original.source_detail: Environmental cleaning: reduce contamination/bioburden between patient-care episodes; reviewed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Replaced the non-specific AORN homepage with CDC's exact OR cleaning procedure. Changed the item from an outcome/bioburden claim to a directly supported practice question and clarified that the between-procedure process concerns environmental surfaces and noncritical equipment.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current CDC environmental-cleaning procedures; NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.claim_audit: CDC explicitly requires OR environmental cleaning between procedures and distinguishes environmental/noncritical equipment from critical/semicritical reprocessing.

distractor_audit.A: CDC does not limit between-case cleaning to visible soil or known infection.
distractor_audit.B: Environmental cleaning does not replace sterile technique.
distractor_audit.D: Terminal cleaning is only one of three intervals, not the only interval.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: C is the only option matching the CDC OR schedule and scope.
audit_findings.cueing: Converted the question to a concrete practice rather than a broad infection-reduction rationale.
audit_findings.blueprint: Environmental infection-control practice fits Safety and Infection Prevention and Control.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked CDC section 4.6.1; C remains uniquely correct.
